items.author: Alicia Haddick

items.text:
An unlikely game has made its way to the top of Steam’s bestsellers list in Japan: a strip mahjong game. Not only has Super Real Mahjong Venus Returns, the latest entry in a series that dates back to PCs and arcades in the late 1980s, become a surprising sales hit, but it’s also become an online obsession on social media as fans share suggestive clips and reminisce about their childhoods playing older entries, something its producer has come to address in a new interview with Automaton West.

This latest entry took a lot of work to bring into existence: news of the planned revival of the series, with support for both traditional screens and VR, came through a Campfire crowdfunding campaign in Japan that raised 33.8 million yen (about $216k), 1690 percent of its goal. The premise is simple; it’s you and four attractive female characters playing mahjong, with victory leading the other characters to remove an article of clothing till they are entirely naked. It’s a simple mix of typical simulated mahjong and sex appeal, but social media has helped propel the release to new heights.

Beginning in the late ’80s, the series found an audience in the arcades with mostly-young and horny teenage boys thanks to its risque content, according to producer Kentaro Matsui, who attributes the game’s existence and success to society being more permissive about sexual content in spaces like arcades at the time of the original game’s release. “From the late 1980s into the 1990s, this country was, for better or worse, an extremely permissive place, and the idea of keeping adult content confined to adult-only spaces barely existed. Japan is sometimes jokingly called ‘the land of hentai,’ and back in the day, strip mahjong genuinely was a nationwide boom.

“There was no chance an impressionable teenager like me would escape that influence. I was completely, hopelessly devoted to those girls. I’d clutch what little pocket money I had, challenge them, and lose again and again. I was left penniless.”

Since its release, fans have spoken up to reminisce about sharing the director’s experience of losing their pocket money trying to win rounds and see the girls strip. “This is Super Real Mahjong!” one user declares. “It was terrifying the way the original game could steal 100yen from young boys in mere seconds.” Another shared a clip of the new entry while reminiscing about the “brotherhood” that would form between teenagers in arcades who would contribute their own money to other players in the hopes they could win and prompt one of the female opponents to remove an article of clothing.

Achieving this was no simple feat, and it’s continued to be challenging in this new title. Successful players have been eager to share clips of their naturally suggestive exploits, with particular love being given to the tomboyish Mizuki Tohno. Those failing can’t help but sigh over how difficult it is to win at the game.

In arcades, the game’s had a win condition such that if you reached a state where the girls would be forced to remove their final article of clothing, it would suddenly end. This was a legal requirement due to the game being played in arcades, but with the new release being placed in the privacy of people’s homes, full nudity can now be achieved. “The moment a girl reached her last piece of clothing [in the original], someone’s parent would walk in, or the next customer would show up, and the scene would cut away,” Matsui recalls. “Going beyond that line was this project’s central mission, and we managed to achieve it.”

The developers chose to make the gameplay scenarios almost identical to those of the original game, focusing more on updating visuals while keeping the characters the same and making some tweaks to gameplay inspired by modern titles like Mahjong Soul and Bunny Garden. That, and introducing VR support to the game, which compliments the now-3D visuals of the game, letting players freely move around the space and the female opponents. “The person undressing is sitting directly across the table from you. You can stand up, lean in, and watch from whatever angle and distance you like. Compared to classic strip mahjong, where you watch a video play out on the far side of a screen, it’s a completely different experience. Originally, we conceived this as a VR-only feature. But realistically, a great many people don’t own a headset, so we built it out properly for Desktop Mode as well.”

All the excitement has seen the game shoot up the Japanese sales charts, where it’s competing with major new releases like Onimusha as one of the best-selling premium games in the country by revenue; separately, its VR-enabling DLC is charting above titles like Palworld and Forza Horizon 6. Sex sells, and in some cases, it can even unite a country!

The series’ legacy was a major factors in this success. “Among the many different strip mahjong games, this series was legendary, and the reason is clear,” explains Matsui. “At a time when static pixel art was the norm, Super Real Mahjong was the one series where the characters moved beautifully and smoothly, almost like in a TV anime. In today’s terms, it felt like an artifact from the future. The moment it’s announced, people can’t help posting their old memories on social media. We actually spent almost nothing on advertising, and we were still fortunate enough to get an enormous amount of attention. It felt less like we did something clever and more like 30 years of accumulated memories erupted all at once.

“While sexy games are hardly uncommon these days, I don’t think Super Real Mahjong was embraced simply because it’s sexy. It never competed on raw explicitness. What people responded to, I suspect, was the act of undressing itself, and the room for imagination left just before and just after it.”

Seeing this “overwhelmingly beautiful and unreasonably strong” series make a comeback has ignited the memories of older fans while making newcomers curious, a perfect storm that social media helped propel to new heights. Notably, this is the first title in the series to be available in English, for anyone who wants to play it for themselves, something that has even led major VTubers to consider giving it a try. The developers have added support to assist mahjong newcomers, including an auto mode, but surely the true satisfaction is in winning via your own skills. Hopefully the interest in Venus Returns drives people to develop their own mahjong skills, and they find getting better at the classic Chinese game of tiles and almost as rewarding as this release’s other draws.

The Legend Of Zelda: Breath Of The Wild Has Landed On PlayStation 5

Nintendo

Published Oct 7, 2026, 5:52 AM EDT

James is a gaming writer from London who has spent thousands of hours exploring titles from every genre. Though he has a particular affinity for multiplayer titles like World of Warcraft, Destiny 2 and League of Legends, he has also put thousands of hours into single-player experiences, from deep RPGs to epic PC strategies. When he's not playing or writing, he can usually be found supporting his beloved Brentford FC.

Of all the franchises that Nintendo has under its belt, very few are as closely associated with the mega developer as The Legend of Zelda. The first game debuted over 40 years ago at this point, and since then, it has only been able to be played on Nintendo's proprietary consoles, whether that be the SNES or the Nintendo Switch 2.

That said, recent times have seen the landscape shift, mostly thanks to the efforts of fans who want to play older games in a more convenient manner. That has led to a glut of older titles making their way over to the PC via both emulation and native ports, all of which make it a lot easier to keep the memory of those games alive.

Now, Zelda has cropped up over on PlayStation, and far from being a retro effort, it's actually one of the most recent games in the series.

As first reported by TweakTown, The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild is now playable in 4K on PlayStation 5 consoles, if you're willing to go through some technical steps. Essentially, the game is running on a jailbroken PlayStation 5 console in 4K at 30 FPS, via the PS5CEMU-HAR emulator.

As the name suggests, that technology adapts the CEMU and Azahar emulators (which are focused on the Wii U and 3DS) for the PlayStation 5. It uses Mihawk's PS5 port of the RADV driver, which adds full support for DualSense controllers, while CEMU does all the heavy lifting to render the game at the PS5's native 4K (3840 x 2160) resolution with upscaling and additional frame pacing.

This adjusted Wii U release looks pretty great and it runs well, even if it is quite far from a legitimate Legend of Zelda release on PlayStation. The fun doesn't stop there either, as it also supports installing community-created graphics and texture packs, with many options available that bring the game much more into line with modern expectations.

The latter is needed a little more as well, chiefly because this is the Wii U version of the game, rather than the Nintendo Switch release. With this approach now a possibility, don't be surprised if modders quickly come up with additional downloads that are designed to take advantage of the PS5's capabilities specifically.

Fans of The Legend of Zelda have plenty to look forward to from official sources as well, even if the community continues to bring out memorabl steps forward. The Ocarina of Time Remake is up first in November, bringing back an all-time classic title for a whole new generation of gamers. That's followed in relatively short order by the big movie adaptation, which is set to drop in April of next year.

James is a gaming writer from London who has spent thousands of hours exploring titles from every genre. Though he has a particular affinity for multiplayer titles like World of Warcraft, Destiny 2 and League of Legends, he has also put thousands of hours into single-player experiences, from deep RPGs to epic PC strategies. When he's not playing or writing, he can usually be found supporting his beloved Brentford FC.

Of all the franchises that Nintendo has under its belt, very few are as closely associated with the mega developer as The Legend of Zelda. The first game debuted over 40 years ago at this point, and since then, it has only been able to be played on Nintendo's proprietary consoles, whether that be the SNES or the Nintendo Switch 2.

That said, recent times have seen the landscape shift, mostly thanks to the efforts of fans who want to play older games in a more convenient manner. That has led to a glut of older titles making their way over to the PC via both emulation and native ports, all of which make it a lot easier to keep the memory of those games alive.
Now, Zelda has cropped up over on PlayStation, and far from being a retro effort, it's actually one of the most recent games in the series.

blocks.x: As first reported by TweakTown, The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild is now playable in 4K on PlayStation 5 consoles, if you're willing to go through some technical steps. Essentially, the game is running on a jailbroken PlayStation 5 console in 4K at 30 FPS, via the PS5CEMU-HAR emulator.

As the name suggests, that technology adapts the CEMU and Azahar emulators (which are focused on the Wii U and 3DS) for the PlayStation 5. It uses Mihawk's PS5 port of the RADV driver, which adds full support for DualSense controllers, while CEMU does all the heavy lifting to render the game at the PS5's native 4K (3840 x 2160) resolution with upscaling and additional frame pacing.

This adjusted Wii U release looks pretty great and it runs well, even if it is quite far from a legitimate Legend of Zelda release on PlayStation. The fun doesn't stop there either, as it also supports installing community-created graphics and texture packs, with many options available that bring the game much more into line with modern expectations.

The latter is needed a little more as well, chiefly because this is the Wii U version of the game, rather than the Nintendo Switch release. With this approach now a possibility, don't be surprised if modders quickly come up with additional downloads that are designed to take advantage of the PS5's capabilities specifically.

items.text:
PlayStation Plus Drops Bonus October 2026 Free Download For New Fantasy RPG

Published Oct 7, 2026, 5:06 AM EDT

Paul Farrelly is a Contributing Writer for Screen Rant’s Gaming section and the founder of GeekGasm.org, a site dedicated to celebrating all things gaming, from triple A blockbusters to weird and wonderful indie hits. Based in Louth, Ireland, Paul has spent years writing about games, pop culture, and tech, turning his lifelong love of gaming into a career that lets him talk (probably too much) about what makes this industry so endlessly fascinating.
He’s previously written and collaborated with several entertainment outlets, including LADbible, gaining a wide perspective on how gaming fits into today’s pop culture conversation. His work blends genuine enthusiasm with thoughtful analysis, exploring how design, storytelling, and community have made gaming one of the most creative mediums around.
When he’s not glued to a controller or keyboard, Paul’s usually spinning vinyl, plotting his next horror marathon, or debating which Resident Evil entry really reigns supreme.

While the free monthly games for PlayStation Plus subscribers is a bit of a mixed bag this October, a bonus gift for Premium members might help turn a lot of nay-sayers around. Souls-like games are swiftly launching all the time, but the truly great ones are still rare commodities. FromSoftware has that magic sauce that many try but fail to replicate. Everything from the animations of the bosses, the audio and visual clues and the feel of the weapons can either make a game special or ruin it for everyone.

So, getting the option to trial one for free with PlayStation Plus at launch sounds like the ideal way to test drive a Souls-like without throwing down hard cash in advance. With Souls-like especially, it's not until you've picked up the controller and played around with the dodge/parry mechanics first until you realize if the game is a good fit for you. It just has to feel right and reading reviews can't really replicate that feeling. For every Elden Ring masterpiece, there's a dozen Immortal: Unchained games to sift through.

Valor Mortis is a Souls-like set in an alternate 19th century filled with horrors for players to try to survive. The game launches on October 13, 2026, and PlayStation Plus Premium members will be able to indulge in a free trial of the game before deciding if a purchase is needed. The trial lasts for 90 minutes, which is a little shorter than typical game trials, but should be just long enough to get a taste of this twisted horror RPG. At a glance, Valor Mortis has visuals and artistic flair for days, with the grotesque twisted army soldiers looking like something only Clive Barker could dream up.

In Valor Mortis, you play as a resurrected soldier who served and died for Napoleon. However, the world you reawaken in is very different from the one you left. Filled with nightmarish monsters with a taste for blood, Valor Mortis leans heavily into survival combat and horror. Each encounter is a chance to master your weapons, improve your parries and hopefully learn more about this twisted historical nightmare set in an alternate 19th century European battlefield.

With many gamers saving their hard-earned cash for games like the fast approaching The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of TIme remake or perhaps the special edition vinyl soundtrack to accompany Grand Theft Auto VI, getting a 'try before you buy' offer like the Valor Mortis game trial feels timely. And although 90 minutes of gameplay doesn't feel particularly generous, it should be enough time to get to that first boss and get a real sense of whether Valor Mortis is a good fit for you.

Valor Mortis is also available on launch for GamePass subscribers, so there are a few ways to get your hands on the 20-hour Napoleonic nightmare on launch day. Will it stack up against the upcoming Nintendo Switch 2 exclusive The Duskbloods? Only time will tell, but with only a few weeks until launch, GamePass subscribers and PlayStation Plus Premium subscribers don't have long to wait to find out if Valor Mortis will find courage in death or just be dead on arrival! All signs point to the former.

items.text:
Summary

Collider's Steve Weintraub talks with Aaron Sorkin for The Social Reckoning.

Sorkin discusses how Facebook has evolved since The Social Network.

The writer-director also comments on legal notes and shaping key scenes in the edit.

Over a decade after Aaron Sorkin wrote The Social Network, the Oscar-winning writer-director returns with a companion feature, The Social Reckoning, about whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison), the Facebook engineer who enlisted the help of a green Wall Street journalist, Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White), to investigate the behemoth company’s questionable intentions.

In the movie, Haugen and Horwitz begin researching Facebook’s shift from a find-your-friends social media platform to a constant newsfeed fueled by an algorithm that churns contention, and the growing concerns and consequences of that evolution. The Social Reckoning also stars Oscar nominee Jeremy Strong (The Apprentice) as billionaire CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Academy Award nominee Wunmi Mosaku (Sinners) as Raya Akinola, Betty Gilpin (Widow’s Bay), Billy Magnussen (Violent Ends), and Bill Burr (Breaking Bad).

In this interview with Collider’s Steve Weintraub, Sorkin clarifies the connection between The Social Network and The Social Reckoning, discusses the “different realities” we’re fed through Facebook, and also comments on just how much legal interference he dealt with throughout the making of the movie. Check out all of this and more in the video above, with a transcript provided below.

Aaron Sorkin on Why There Won't Be Government Regulation of Big Tech

And how he dodged interference in his movie.

Image via Sony Pictures

COLLIDER: I'm doing a supercut right now, and the question is, where do you like to sit in a movie theater?

AARON SORKIN: You know what? For me, there isn't a bad seat in a movie theater. I don't even mind sitting in the front row. But I guess if I could pick any seat, it would be halfway up on an aisle.

You're an aisle person.

SORKIN: Yeah. I don't know, I like the security of the aisle. But again, I'm happy sitting in any seat.

Thank you for indulging me on the question. Jumping into why I get to talk to you. Your film shines a very important light on Meta, who owns Facebook and Instagram. My big thing is, what do you think it's going to take for governments and our government to do anything to curb the misinformation that exists online, which your film brilliantly points out?

SORKIN: Listen, they can pass laws, but the problem is that there are about five tech oligarchs who are financing the campaigns of the people who pass laws, and that's why it's not going to happen, or that's why it hasn't happened.

It's incredibly frustrating.

SORKIN: Yes.

It makes me so angry. I would imagine that when you're making something like this, you are possibly going to run into a wall where a lawyer says you cannot include this, so was there anything that you really wanted to include that lawyers were like, “Nope?”

SORKIN: No. Listen, under normal circumstances, there'd be a thorough legal vetting of a script of a nonfiction movie. In this case, they wouldn't hire an outside law firm just to concentrate on this film. There were notes, but nothing that hurt me. Changing somebody's name, that kind of thing. Little things, a few numbers, but nothing that hurt me. The lawyers, I'm happy to say, wanted us to make the film we wanted to make.

How Facebook Went From a Site for Friends to a World of "Different Realities"

"None of which, by the way, is being fact-checked."

Image via Sony Pictures

Image via Sony Pictures

Image via Sony Pictures

Close

If people sit down in the future and watch Social Network and Social Reckoning back to back, what do you hope the conversations are that they're having when the two films are over?

SORKIN: Well, first, let me say, I know there's been discussion about whether The Social Reckoning is a sequel, that kind of thing. It's another movie about Facebook, written by the same writer who wrote The Social Network, and one of the characters from The Social Network is in The Social Reckoning, sort of as if Henry Hill showed up in Casino.

If they watched the two movies back to back, I think the conversation would have to be about, “Well, wait… What changed? In 2010, it was this site where you kept track of your friends, and now it's something else.” Well, what changes is that they added the newsfeed. And once they added a newsfeed that was powered by an algorithm, it meant you were getting the news that you want while I was getting the news that I want, and she's getting the news she wants. We're all living in different realities — none of which, by the way, is being fact-checked.

"Sony received letters from Meta."

Related

I'm fascinated by the editing process because it's where it all comes together. You have these brilliant actors delivering these amazing takes. Talk a little bit about how the film was shaped in the editing room, possibly in a way you didn't expect. Did you end up with a lot of deleted scenes? I'm fascinated by the process.

SORKIN: Yeah, me too. Our editor, Alan Baumgarten, did a fantastic job with his post-production team. There isn't very much on the cutting room floor. A line here and there. I would say that certainly the climactic scene of the film, which I don't want to give away too much now, I knew that that was going to be something that was shaped in the editing. But we shot most of that on our first two days of shooting, and Alan would call me from the editing room saying, “It's going to work. It's going to work. This is cutting together. It's going to work.”

The Social Reckoning opens in theaters on October 9.

items.text:
Published Oct 7, 2026, 1:00 AM EDT

Nicholas Becher is a gaming journalist with an MFA in Creative Writing from FAU. With extensive experience playing video games, he covers all forms of gaming content at Screen Rant, from breaking news to the latest fan theories. Most-played games range from Clair Obscur to Civ to Elden Ring to Halo 2 and beyond.

James S.A. Corey (aka Daniel Abraham and Ty Franck) created a truly original sci-fi adventure with The Expanse that was built around a not-so-unrealistic future vision of our own society. It's one that was adapted into a cult favorite television series with such an enthusiastic following that they managed to save it from certain doom. After Syfy canceled The Expanse following its third season, the series found a new home on Prime Video after a major revival campaign, where it continued for another three seasons before reaching its conclusion in 2022.

However, the original novels extend well beyond the point where the television adaptation ended, leaving plenty of unexplored stories and characters in various corners of the solar system for the franchise to revisit someday. Fans hoping to return to that universe fortunately won't have to wait much longer, as The Expanse is officially making its return in 2027 and bringing audiences a brand-new story that promises another journey into its dangerous vision of humanity's future, albeit in an unconventional medium.

The Expanse Returns Yet Again In 2027

The Expanse's long-awaited return comes in 2027 courtesy of Osiris Reborn, a new third-person action RPG from Owlcat Games, the studio behind Pathfinder: Wrath of the Righteous and Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader. While it doesn't adapt one of James S.A. Corey's novels directly, Osiris Reborn tells an original story within the established universe, with an emphasis on decision-making, unique and original companions/NPCs, exploration, and squad-based combat.

Importantly, this isn't a sequel to the television show's sixth and final season, as Osiris Reborn instead takes place alongside the early events of The Expanse, beginning around the Eros crisis and overlapping roughly with the show's first two-and-a-half seasons. It gives Owlcat room to play with familiar locations and events while following an entirely different group of characters rather than simply putting players in control of Holden and the Rocinante crew and rehashing the same story over again.

Players create their own captain, choosing an Earther, Martian, or Belter background (of course), while the game's new ensemble includes the protagonist's identical twin, J, alongside original companions such as mechanic Zafar, mercenary Michael, and medic Teo. Each crew member has their own personality, a specified role aboard the ship, and their own unique combat abilities, meaning you'll have to utilize the crew and learn their strengths/weaknesses if you want to survive.

The Expanse: Osiris Reborn Tells An Original Story In A Familiar Timeline

The Expanse: Osiris Reborn has a great opportunity to give players a brand-new experience in a familiar timeline of its already established universe. The game runs parallel to some of the most important events from the beginning of show, allowing players to experience things through an entirely new group of characters' perspectives. Developers have placed the story across roughly the first two-and-a-half seasons of the television series, meaning the destruction of the Canterbury, the Eros disaster, and the growing tensions between Earth, Mars, and the Belt all serve as a backdrop.

Players begin as a Pinkwater Security mercenary visiting Eros alongside their identical twin, J. Unfortunately, they happen to be there as the station descends into chaos, forcing the pair to escape aboard an experimental ship while losing friends and colleagues in the process. That escape ultimately puts the new crew in the middle of a much larger conspiracy and gives Owlcat its own storyline without needing to substantially alter Holden's established journey or retcon anything and upset hardcore fans.

Players will travel to recognizable locations including Ceres, Mars, Luna, and Ganymede while witnessing how the events from the show affect people elsewhere in the solar system. Owlcat has also teased encounters with recognizable characters, creating opportunities for the game's new cast to cross paths with characters fans already know and love/loath.

The Expanse: Osiris Reborn is scheduled for spring 2027, with Steam currently narrowing that to Q2 2027. It will launch on PS5, Xbox Series X/S, and PC through Steam, Epic Games Store, and GOG, with Xbox Game Pass availability starting on day one.

items.title: Zach Cregger Is Making Everyone Want to Play the Resident Evil Games
items.author: Brianne Garbutt
items.summary: Fans of Barbarian and Weapons likely weren’t surprised to find out that Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil film was another smash hit, capturing the feel of the
items.text:
Fans of Barbarian and Weapons likely weren’t surprised to find out that Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil film was another smash hit, capturing the feel of the iconic survival horror franchise while offering a brand-new story and protagonist.

Introducing Bryan, his green cooler, and his sheep beanie

Following its September 18 release, Resident Evil has brought in a whopping $245 million at the worldwide box office, blowing its own $75 million budget out of the water. Similar to Cregger’s previous offerings – of his recent films, Barbarian lags behind at a 92% Rotten Tomatoes rating – Resident Evil earned a 96% rating on the Tomatometer, and a 91% rating on the Popcornmeter, proving to delightfully disgust critics and audiences alike.

Starring Austin Abrams as Bryan, a thirty-something courier just trying to make a little extra cash, Resident Evil plunges its audience into a frantic dash through Raccoon City that doesn’t let up until the credits roll. The supporting cast of characters includes an excellent turn from Paul Walter Hauser as an unnamed Umbrella employee, clearly if not understandably out of his depth; Isla McRae as the little girl Bryan stumbles upon as she cowers in an RV, all alone for a pretty good reason; and Cregger himself, credited simply as “the voice on the intercom” that Bryan speaks to when he finally reaches his destination.

The horror and gore is broken up with just the right amount of humor and heart, especially where Bryan himself is concerned. Audiences root for Bryan, just as they root for familiar protagonists like Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield. His goal, apart from making his last delivery of the night, is to make it back to girlfriend Michelle, who has just learned she is pregnant with Bryan’s baby.

Cregger’s excellent movie inspired new players to pick up the game

What sets Cregger’s film apart from the franchise films which came before it is, yes, it takes audiences back to Raccoon City during the middle of an outbreak – the infamous Raccoon City Incident – but it also manages to capture the feeling of playing a Resident Evil game for the first time. Bryan is both a rookie (no pun intended, Leon) player and one of those NPCs whose journal entries and voice memos players find scattered around the city. The film pays homage to the games without being derivative, acting more than anything else as a love letter to the franchise. A love letter likely spattered with gore, true, but loving nonetheless.

In fact, Cregger did such a good job in recreating the feeling of playing a Resident Evil game that the audience wanted more after the 95-minute runtime of the movie. Game sales for the Resident Evil 2 and Resident Evil 4 remakes have seen an increase across multiple platforms. On Playstation, RE2 – which, like the movie, takes place in Raccoon City – saw a 64% increase in sales, with a smaller 11% boost on Steam. Resident Evil 4 also saw boosted sales, with a 54% increase in sales on PS5, followed by a 14% increase on Steam. And that’s without taking the sales on either platform into consideration, which saw the prices of the games jump down to $9.99 or less.

What was it about Cregger’s movie that gave game sales a boost?

Especially with sales going on at the same time, it might be difficult to ascertain just how Zach Cregger’s film has played a part in Resident Evil 2 and Resident Evil 4 seeing an increase in their sales numbers. Still, it’s clear that the movie played a part, and the reason why might be found in the originality of the film.

There are Easter eggs scattered throughout the movie, including two health sprays in the barn where Bryan shelters from an overly non-friendly dog, but for the most part, the only familiar names are Raccoon City and the Umbrella Corporation. Bryan’s story is meant to take place alongside the action of Resident Evil 2, and that comes across loud and clear. It’s a taste of what the games can offer, albeit one that is rich in flavor.

Along with entries in the gaming franchise like this year’s Resident Evil 9: Requiem and Resident Evil 7: Biohazard (2017), both of which feature fresh protagonists, Cregger’s Resident Evil film proves that audiences are capable of embracing what is new, as long as the soul of the franchise remains.

items.title: Excuse Me, Square Enix, Where The Hell Is Cid’s Chest Hair In Final Fantasy VII Revelation?
items.author: Kenneth Shepard

items.text:
Square Enix put out a few new clips from Final Fantasy VII Revelation that feel laser-targeted at me, the type of player who isn’t swayed by big open worlds or a conclusion to a story I think has been laughably inconsistent. You know what does draw me to the third game in Square Enix’s Remake trilogy? The lovable goofballs in its party. You know what’s even better at getting me to pay attention? Seeing the men in the group in their new bathing suits in the game’s hot-springs sections. That’s right, after giving the ladies their fanservice moment in Rebirth with their cute swimsuits in Costa del Sol, the men are getting some sun, and the boy likers are getting some eye candy with costumes that players will be able to unlock and use throughout the game, according to director Naoki Hamaguchi. But…wait…why is Cid as smooth as Cloud’s twink ass?

The two clips show a couple of humorous scenes of the party in hot springs together. One shows Cloud, Red XIII, and Barret trying to balance rubber chocobos on their heads, and the other has Barret and Cid stumbling upon Vincent bathing in full combat armor. For all my problems with the Remake trilogy, I have to admit it excels in fun moments like this. You can tell Square Enix loves these characters and riffing on their dynamics in cute ways in between all the big emotional swings and all the mini-game bloat. So I’m sure when we get these scenes in English, the voice cast will make them really sing for those of us who can’t understand the Japanese we hear in these clips. But I’m here to talk about what I can see instead of what’s being said, and Square Enix, I have some feedback.

Barret is perfect. No notes, actually. You’re making up for sticking him in a sailor suit in Rebirth when he could have been showing off his beefy ripped self like god intended, and I appreciate it. It’s Cid that I take issue with. Rather than making the grizzled world’s-oldest-32-year-old a hairy-chested daddy like he should be, Square Enix has made this dude a hairless twink. I know you took away his cigarettes, Square, but he can still have a little bit of ruggedness, as a treat (for me).

Some games just straight up don’t have body hair on any character models, a limitation I’ve lamented in games like Dragon Age: The Veilguard, which lets you really customize your character but makes everyone from the twinkiest elf to the burliest dwarf smooth below the neck. But Final Fantasy VII Revelation and its predecessors don’t fall into this category. Barret has a hairy chest, so Square’s clearly not shying away from putting it in the game as a rule. It was refreshing when Wolverine went out of its way to make its claw-wielding hero hairy in just about every place he should be (though, what, does he shave his pits or something?) and constantly showcased it as his armor was torn apart in fights. So now when I see Cid, who is allegedly 32 but in actuality 47, looking like his body is the same as Cloud’s, I want to sit someone at Square Enix down and say, “hey, spiritually, this man should have a fuzzy chest, and I think we all know this. Revelation isn’t out on PC, PS5, Switch 2, and Xbox Series X/S until April 8, so there is time to rectify this.”

When this format of monitor based on Samsung's QD-OLED panel tech originally appeared in 2024, you were looking around $1,200. Now it's yours for less than half the price.

This particular model runs at a "mere" 165 Hz rather than the 240 Hz of more expensive variants. But then the idea that you're going to be running demanding games at 240 fps-plus at 4K is pretty implausible.

What you don't lose out on with this cheapest of 4K OLEDs is the bananas 0.03 ms response time, the perfect per-pixel lighting, the incredibly punchy colours of QD-OLED tech, all enhanced by the elevated pixel density of 4K.

Inevitably, this is a first-gen 4K QD-OLED panel with 250 nits full-screen and 1,000 nits peak HDR brightness. The latest 32-inch 4K QD-OLEDs are a touch brighter. And the USB-C input is limited to 15 W of power delivery. But make no mistake, this remains one of the great PC gaming experiences.

items.title: Gundam Rogue Orbit gave me a sick whip sword, but held back the one thing I want most in a mech game
items.author: wesley@pcgamer.com (Wes Fenlon)
items.summary: I didn't know I could have an entitled opinion about giant anime robots until I played a preview of Gundam Rogue Orbit, but it turns out I can. I'm mad
items.text:
I didn't know I could have an entitled opinion about giant anime robots until I played a preview of Gundam Rogue Orbit, but it turns out I can. I'm mad because they gave me a Gundam with a whip sword straight out of Bloodborne (if Gundam hadn't actually gotten there first in the mid-'90s).

To be clear, I'm not mad at the whip sword itself. I'm ecstatic about the whip sword. It's exactly the kind of esoteric weapon that suggests Rogue Orbit has a real shot at being the kind of action game that I want out of Gundam—one with a bit more melee crunch and nuance than they tend to offer. But I can't help but look this gift sword in the mouth, because months after revealing the game, the Gundam team are still holding back hands-on with the bit I want to see most: a damn customization screen.

Why couldn't I look through a short list of weapons whitelisted for the demo build and have a chance to think: "Whip sword? Yes, I'll be having some of that." The fact that you can customize your mech in Rogue Orbit isn't secret: there's a screenshot of the menu on the freaking Steam page! Here's what it looks like:

Bandai NamcoBandai NamcoBandai NamcoThat looks cool. I would've loved to spend at least a few seconds pondering stats like "close-range power" and "output" before deciding a 60-foot-tall robot using a whip to channel its inner Belmont while fighting aliens is far too dope to resist, numbies be damned.

Demos always have to strike a balance between showing too much and not enough, risking a confusing amount of up-front complexity or a slice so thin it misses some of the fatty goodness that adds flavor. I played about 30 minutes of Rogue Orbit, which was all action, accompanied by plenty of anime-tinged voiceover about the aliens(?) called "The Apocalypse" that made me think I will probably not pay much attention to anything that happens in this story.

On the edginess scale, though, Rogue Orbit's got nothing on the likes of "XXXG-01D2 Gundam Deathscythe Hell" from Gundam Wing: Endless Waltz—you can practically feel the impending turn of the millennium oozing from every letter in that cursed name. Rogue Orbit may not be the politically tinged deliberation on war I love from the best Gundam shows, but that's okay—it's doing something different, and the combo-heavy action immediately made me feel like the game was on to something.

Rogue Orbit skews a bit more action RPG than Devil May Cry—the combos are just a few repeated button presses, and much of your damage comes from throwing in active skills which each have their own cooldowns. Holding a trigger and tapping Square on a PlayStation pad made my Gundam swirl the whip sword around in a 360 degree frenzy, catching anyone nearby in a flurry of quick hits.

Another weapon, the Sword Lance, almost felt Monster Hunter-inspired, building up a unique meter every time I performed a heavy lunging attack mid-dodge. That meter could then be spent to spawn a "Beam Phalanx" of laser-spewing orbs.

Damage numbers, on by default, increase the sense that in the full game I'll be monitoring skill cooldowns a la Granblue Fantasy: Relink as much as I am focusing on attack timing or perfect dodges.

This is, nevertheless, the closest any Gundam game I've ever played has felt like FromSoftware's sublime Armored Core 6. A gentler, "have fun pressing buttons and watch shiny particles go everywhere" cousin, to be sure, but a cousin nonetheless.

It's sort of a cute full-circle moment: In the pre-Dark Souls days, FromSoftware developed several Gundam games for Bandai Namco around the same time it was putting out Armored Core: For Answer and Armored Core 5. The learner has become the master, and so on. If the current Gundam dev team looked at AC6 with envy and decided to replicate it for a slightly less hardcore audience, I think that was a wise move, and I also think, at least based on my early impressions, that they've pulled it off.

But it still feels like I haven't seen the most important bit. So much of the joy of Armored Core—of any proper mech game, really—is assembling a build before tackling a mission, trying to find that balance of speed and durability, raw damage and ammo capacity, range and up-close stopping power that fits the coming threat.

(Image credit: Bandai Namco)Demo practicality be damned—until I'm putting that whip sword in my Gundam's hand myself, I won't know for certain if this is the next great mech action game or not. The full game is out in March.

items.title: "Coders will never forgive me for this level": Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 has a rotatable "fleshmetal" puzzle map that drove its own development team crazy
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: In the grim darkness of the far future, there is something far worse than war. There is: a level that is basically a huge, spinning lock full of tentacles,
items.text:
In the grim darkness of the far future, there is something far worse than war. There is: a level that is basically a huge, spinning lock full of tentacles, with your Space Marine or Sister of Battle protagonist naturally serving as the key.

Auroch Digital's new FPS Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 launches next week, and I've been chatting to the game's principal designer Matt Bone about some of the more "creative" environments in store. It's a sturdy rule of thumb that all the best ideas in gamedev are the ones that make your colleagues want to fill your trousers with sea urchins. Bone certainly appears to have achieved this with the map comfortingly known as Vicious Circles.

Watch on YouTube

"One of the things we wanted to do with Boltgun 2 is add more variety," he told me over email. "Part of that is more diverse and exotic biomes, and another part is introducing novel mechanics. The level 'Vicious Circles' is a great example of this, and definitely one of the more challenging levels to make. The informal name the team uses for the level is 'Puzzle Box', as it's made up of a series of connected, rotating 'ring' sections, as well as a giant, slowly spinning cog that acts as the finale of the level. The player moves one of the rings at different points in the levels, unlocking different areas so that they can progress (or explore for secrets).

"These moving sections are covered in enemies and pickups, which is part of the reason coders will never forgive me for this level," Bone went on. "Getting enemies to reliably navigate and fight the player on moving, interconnected platforms is a bit of a headache, as you can imagine. And spinning a gigantic cog covered in hundreds of meshes is quite the performance challenge."

Not content with alienating the coders, Bone has also managed to earn the eternal enmity of the art team. The Vicious Circles level is set in a spaceship belonging to Boltgun 2's primary antagonist Vashtorr, a demigod who – as is often the pastime of Chaos denizens – really enjoys building machines out of body parts and vice versa. "We really leaned into this 'fleshmetal' aspect for the environment, which looks incredible and appropriately disturbing," Bone went on. "But the reason artists now also hate me is that all of this intricate level art has to work in multiple configurations, not just one. A wriggling fleshy tendril may look perfect in the original level layout, but has to then avoid clipping through walls in the level's various rotations."

"Whilst it was certainly a challenge, I absolutely think it was worth it," he concluded, with the resolute good cheer of a man reconciled to his own damnation. "Hopefully it'll be a memorable level for players!"

Speaking as one such feckless player, I feel no sympathy for Auroch Digital's rank-and-file. I've just been reading the papers, and according to some columnist or other, you've all been 'corrupting the children' - being forced to make a massive Merry-go-Round out of gall bladders is no more than you deserve. Also, I really like videogame levels that are ginormous machines, such as the Clockwork Mansion in Dishonored 2, or Anoat City (kind of) in Star Wars: Dark Forces, or Into The Abyss from Titanfall 2. Any other favourite or especially loathed examples to share?

Read more about Boltgun 2 on Steam. Here is what Caelyn thought of the first: "A fast and joyously entertaining rampage through a spot-on recreation of the Warhammer 40,000 setting, Boltgun is the FPS that 40k fans have dreamed of since the first time they inexpertly splodged too-thick paint all over a Space Marine. Pacing issues can’t prevent it from being a bloody good time."

items.title: 35 English Loanwords That Come From the Japanese Language
items.author: Coto Academy Staff Writer
items.summary: While Japanese has tons of English loanwords, English actually borrows quite a bit from Japanese as well. Words like sushi, karate, or tsunami are so commonly
items.text:
While Japanese has tons of English loanwords, English actually borrows quite a bit from Japanese as well. Words like sushi, karate, or tsunami are so commonly used that it might be easy to forget that they’re loanwords from Japan.

Let’s discover some common Japanese loanwords in English, covering some of the old and some of the new, but this blog is by no means exhaustive. By the end of this article, who knows? New words are probably being borrowed at this very moment.

Why Do Japanese and English Borrow so Many Words From Each Other?

Since Japanese and English come from very different places with distinct cultures, cuisines, and geographic characteristics or phenomena, the more exposed we are to each other’s cultures, the more new concepts and words we encounter. It makes sense that English would just adopt the words for Japanese food items like “sushi” or “ramen.”

However, the word tsunami is also of Japanese origin. It just so happens that English had no word for huge tidal waves, so it borrowed tsunami from Japanese. Often when a word sufficiently describes something we don’t have a word for, we just adopt it into our language. As you are probably well aware, Japanese quite often does the same.

You’ve probably experienced what could be called the katakana glitch. You see a katakana word, and you just can’t figure out what it is until you mouth it, then you finally figure out that biiru (ビール) is actually “beer”. You probably can think of many more English loanwords in Japanese, such as soccer, or sakkaa (サッカー), and even modern slang like rizz, or rizu (リズ). New words are crossing over, perhaps because the internet and pop culture spread new trends faster than ever before.

Note that this doesn’t always happen; when baseball was introduced to Japan, they made their own word for the sport, yakyuu (野球), which is made up of the words field, or 野 (ya), and ball, 球 (kyuu).

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Food and Entertainment

In 2013, UNESCO named Japanese food an intangible cultural heritage. The flavors and practices associated with Japanese food are unique. Many of the Japanese loanwords in English reflect that uniqueness. Similarly, many aspects of Japanese entertainment tend to originate in Japan, and the English words borrowed from Japanese show that.

A lot of these loanwords are originally written in kanji, hiragana, or katakana. If you need to review hiragana and katakana, head to this article.

1. Karaoke (カラオケ)

Did you even know this was a Japanese word before Karaoke actually came into contact with Japan or the language? It has roots in the words: kara (空), meaning “empty,” and oke (オケ), meaning “orchestra.” So, together the word actually means orchestraAlso, have you seen anyone do karaoke like the Japanese?

2. Sudoku (すどく)

If you’ve played sudoku and understand it, more power to you. This game and its title originated in Japan in 1984 and have since become very popular worldwide. The su comes from suji or suu (数), meaning number, and the doku (独) means single. The overall aim of the game is to get numbers to appear once in squares in a grid. So literally, the numbers must remain single. Or suuji wa dokushin ni kagiru (数字は独身に限る), which was the original title of the game.

Europeans actually played a similar game in the 18th century. In the 1980s, a Japanese publisher distributed sudoku, which turned into a huge hit and has been popular ever since.

3. Pachinko　(パチンコ)

Hard to spend any time in Japan and not see a pachinko parlor. Pachinko is a kind of pinball game played in arcade games or, more commonly, gambling parlors. Japanese people like to make words that mimic or represent the sound you hear, like the bees buzzing or the snake hissing. The word pachinko is partly made up of a Japanese onomatopoeia. The first part, pachin, is from the sound that the metal pinball makes as it hits an obstacle. The ko is a diminutive suffix that means something like ‘little’.

4. Soy (sauce, beans)

Tofu and miso are obviously Japanese loanwords, but soy? Yes, apparently it comes from しょうゆ (shoyu), which is Japanese for soy sauce. The actual Japanese term for the bean is daizu. Edamame, which are green soybeans, is also commonly used in English.

5. Tamari (たまりしょうゆ)

This one is kind of hip these days. Many recipe bloggers suggest using tamari as a ‘healthy’ alternative to regular soy sauce. Tamari is richer, thicker, and less salty than regular soy sauce, but it is also made from fermented soybeans.

6. Shiitake, maitake, matsutake, and enoki mushrooms (椎茸、舞茸、松茸、えのき)

Did I miss any? Many Japanese mushroom names have been carried over and used as-is in English. The most popular of these might be shiitake, which is often pronounced without the second ‘i’, resulting in shitake.

7. Umami (旨味)

Umami is probably one of the most popular Japanese loanwords in English, being used all the time to describe a distinct savory flavor. This term is a relatively recent adoption into the English language, and it’s somewhat new to Japanese as well.

The word was first coined in 1908 when a Japanese scientist used the word to describe the “5th taste,” which is savoriness. In both Japanese and English, umami generally describes the savory flavor you would find in cooked meats, soy sauce, and mushrooms.

8. Dashi　(だし)

No mention of washoku can exclude dashi, stock made from fish or kelp that is used as the base for many Japanese dishes. Dashi is commonly used in English to mean the same thing.

9. Katsu (curry or chicken katsu)　(かつ)

Katsu refers to cutlets of meat that are breaded using panko and deep-fried. The cutlets are usually pork or chicken. Katsu is served with a sauce or with curry. In fact, in some places overseas, katsu curry has become so popular that the term is used to mean all Japanese curry.

10. Panko　(パン粉)

You might have guessed this from the previous entry, but panko is breadcrumbs. They are commonly used in Japanese cooking and the product and the name have crossed over into English-speaking cultures.

The word panko is actually a combination of a loanword that didn’t come from English and the original Japanese word. “Pan” came from the Portuguese language, pao, and ko (粉) is a Japanese word that means “flour” or “dust”.

The biggest difference between panko and standard breadcrumbs is that panko is made from bread without crusts. Panko’s crustless white bread is coarsely ground into airy, large flakes that give fried foods a light, crunchy coating.

11. Amazake (甘酒)

Making the list of words of Japanese origin recently recorded in the Oxford English Dictionary, amazake is a sweet, fermented drink made from rice. Unlike sake, which is also made from rice, amazake is not alcoholic. It literally means sweet (ama) sake.

12. Manga (漫画)

These loanwords are used the same way in English as they are in Japanese. One distinction is that while manga means comics in general in Japan, the term typically means Japanese comics in English.

13. Anime (アニメ)

Probably the most popular loanword used all the time in English is アニメ (anime), which ironically comes from the word “animation” borrowed from English. But in English, “anime” specifically refers to Japanese animation even though in Japanese it refers to all animation. This term is a great example of words being traded back and forth between two languages.

14. Emoji　(絵文字)

Texting and instant messaging is just not the same without emoji, graphics that help express an emotion when words are just not enough. But the cute, yellow pictogram you’ve been using on your iPhone? The word came from the Japanese language. The kanji 絵 (え) means “picture” and 文字 (もじ) means “character” or “letter.” You might learn some new emoji from the Emojipedia online.

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Sport and Martial Arts

Japanese martial arts are known the world over by their Japanese names. These are quite established loanwords, and the sports themselves continue to gain devotees.

15. Judo　(柔道)

Japanese martial arts are well-known throughout the English-speaking world, by their Japanese names. Judo, a defensive martial art, is no exception. The term originates from soft, gentle (柔; juu) and way, road (道; do). Judo is an Olympic event, and practitioners are usually called judoka (柔道家).

When you’re saying the word “judo” in Japanese, remember to elongate the first syllable: Ju-u-dou. In English, however, you can shorten it.

16. Jujutsu　(柔術)

Precursor to judo, this is also a Japanese unarmed martial art. The first part of the term, juu means gentle, just like in judo and the jutsu (術) means skill or art. There are variant spellings in English, including jiu-jitsu or ju-jitsu. It is also the origin of the name of the famous martial art, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu.

However, historical evidence shows that Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu (BJJ) comes from Judo, but at the time Judo was still being called “Ju-Jutsu,” which is why BJJ has its name today rather than “Brazilian Judo.”

17. Karate　(空手)

Karate is definitely one of those Japanese loanwords that almost feels like it’s always been in English. The term originates from empty (kara) and hand (te), meaning fighting with bare hands. But the history actually gets more interesting.

Karate originates with the indigenous people of Okinawa, who referred to their martial arts as 手(te or tii in Okinawan). But because the Okinawans traded so much with China, Chinese martial arts heavily influenced Karate, so it was initially called “Chinese hand” (唐手), pronounced the same as we know it today. Eventually, after Japan took over Okinawa, the name was changed to 空手 (karate).

18. Kendo　(剣道)

Another Japanese martial art that was simply imported into English, it consists of participants using bamboo swords and wearing protective gear based loosely on samurai armor. Ken means “sword” and do means “way.”

19. Sumo　(相撲)

Often suffixed with ‘wrestling’ in English, sumo means to fight. It’s not just the word that has crossed borders. Many non-Japanese people have succeeded as sumo wrestlers, in what is perceived to be a closed and very traditional world. Check out this quick guide to sumo related terms to learn a bit more about the sport.

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Performing and Literary Arts

From the theater to the page, traditional Japanese performing and literary arts have become well-known in English-speaking cultures.

20. Kabuki　(歌舞伎)

This is a kind of Japanese theater. The Online Etymology Dictionary cites two possible origins of this Japanese loanword. One is that kabuki comes from the verb kabuku, meaning to deviate. The first kabuki performance was given in a shrine by a girl, dressed as a man, which was outside of the norm. The other explanation is that kabuki means ‘art of song and dance,’ from ka (song), bu (dance), and ki (art, skill).

21. Noh　(能)

In Noh theater, performers sing and dance while wearing masks. This loanword comes from the Japanese meaning ‘talent’.

22. Tanka　(短歌)

A poem written using just five lines, tanka means short (tan) song (ka). In English, the poems typically use five lines and 31 syllables, but in Japanese, they are typically written in three lines.

23. Haiku (俳句)

If you’ve heard about haiku, you probably have the impression that it takes immense skill to craft them. These poems are written using a set number of syllables. The haiku consists of three lines, with five syllables in the first line, seven in the second, and five in the third.

Though haiku were originally written in Japanese, English poems following this pattern also go by the same name. Literally meaning light (haikai no) verse (ku), these poems are often about nature.

23. Senryu (川柳)

Senryu is a loanword that refers to another type of Japanese poetry that’s similar to haiku. It tends to talk about people, rather than nature. This form was named after a poet who frequently practiced it.

Other Japanese Loanwords We Use in English

From business to bedding and natural disasters, Japanese loanwords are used in many areas of life. The following words don’t fall neatly into the categories we have here. But they are still commonly used.

25. Tycoon (大君)

You’ve probably heard this word used a lot with another t-word, tech, as in tech tycoon. Its origins have little do with technology, however. Taikun was the name foreigners gave to the shogun (another loanword) when they came to Japan in the 1800s. Over time, taikun (great lord) became tycoon. Today, the word refers to someone of tremendous wealth and power.

26. Honcho　(班長)

This is another loanword often used alliteratively with head, as in head honcho, meaning leader. The term originates from Japanese han (group) and cho (leader), and was apparently picked up by foreigners in Japan during the second world war.

27. Skosh (少し: Sukoshi)

Have you ever noticed someone saying, “Just a skosh.” Maybe you’re asking if you need to add more salt when you are making soup. This loanword is a shortening of the Japanese sukoshi, meaning a little. It was adopted by the US servicemen when they were stationed in Japan after World War II. 28. Zen　(善)

This loanword originates from the Japanese school of Zen Buddhism that focuses on meditation. In common use in English, zen means calm and peaceful, and doesn’t explicitly refer to Buddhism.

29. Futon　(布団)

Futon is one of those loanwords that perhaps many people have forgotten is, in fact, a loanword. It’s used to describe a flat mattress that can be rolled up, which is traditional bedding in Japan. However, in English, people refer to couches that have pull-out beds as futons. The fu in this loanword means sheet or cloth, and the ton means group.

Ikigai, as a concept, has been making waves in the English-speaking world in recent years. Iki means life and gai means value, so the term translates to ‘reason for being’. The idea is that with a reason for being or a purpose, people can live more fulfilling lives, as those lives get longer.

31. Tsunami (津波)

Originating from harbor (tsu) and wave (nami), this word has been in use in many unfortunate circumstances recently. As with the original Japanese, it describes a large sea wave caused by an earthquake. Tsunami has also been used in a figurative sense to mean a large and sudden amount of something.

32. Samurai (侍)

Many words from Japanese history are usually adopted directly into English, and samurai is no exception. Samurai describes a specific warrior class that only existed in the context of Japan. Calling them “Japanese knights” just wouldn’t capture what they were and the place they had in Japanese society.

Likewise, many other historical Japanese terms for different social positions or figures, like shogun, daimyo, or even ninja, are simply borrowed in English.

33. Katana (刀)

While katana actually just means “sword,” in English it has come to refer to the specific Japanese sword with its characteristic curved blade that was used by the samurai. Likely due to its unique aesthetics, carefully crafted by skilled blacksmiths, it caught the attention of foreigners. Thus, now we use the word katana to describe the iconic sword from Japan.

The kimono is a beautiful, elegant garment that has come to be known as the national dress of Japan. So, there’s no question why English adopted the word kimono to describe this iconic piece of clothing. There isn’t even an equivalent type of clothing to the kimono in English-speaking countries; while there are dresses and robes, none of them are quite a kimono.

While English has the word “bullet train,” it’s not uncommon for people to opt to use the word “shinkansen” instead. items.text:
If you have started learning Japanese or thinking about doing it soon, you might ask yourself: How long does it take to learn Japanese? It’s an honest question, and probably the most important. Between people’s fascination with Japanese culture and the desire to live in Japan, Japanese has become one of the most popular languages to learn – but also the hardest, too.

The answer to this question is, “it depends”. Understandably, no one likes to hear that — but it’s an honest answer because there’s no one-size-fits-all when it comes to how long it takes to learn Japanese. On a complete beginner-to-advanced scale, it takes around 180 to 1,2000 hours to learn Japanese. In reality, people with no prior kanji knowledge often take more time to learn Japanese thanthose who have.

In this response, we’ll explore the factors that can affect how long it takes to learn Japanese and provide estimates of how long it may take a beginner to become proficient.

Defining Fluency in Japanese Language Learning

To the majority, language fluency is a spectrum. You can talk to your Japanese friends in casual Japanese and call it fluent. You might think that to be one means being able to lead a meeting with your coworkers in full keigo.

A good rule of thumb is if you find yourself constantly translating between Japanese and your own native language and forming sentences quickly, you’d be hard-pressed to describe yourself as fluent. In its academic definition, made by Dr. Paul Nation and Asuza Yamamoto, fluency is ‘being able to receive and produce language at a reasonable rate’. You should ask yourself, “Am I at ease when I speak Japanese? Do I get constantly worried about the next question from my partner?”

On the other hand, this number begs the question: Can I call myself fluent if I can watch anime without subtitles? Can I talk to my Japanese friends without fillers like eto or ano? Or write a foolproof business email to your Japanese boss?

Remember that there’s more to communication than speaking and listening! Japanese language fluency also includes four aspects: speaking, listening, reading, and writing. You may be excellent at conversing in Japanese, but barely able to write a single kanji.

So depending on how you define fluency, you might get to that point faster or slower! And don’t worry: we’ve broken down the study hours based on your goal and the desired level below.

How Long Does it Take to Learn Japanese Based on Your Goal?

The FSI of the US State Department estimates that it takes 88 weeks, or 2,200 study hours, to reach what most people define as Japanese fluency. This is probably a fairer assessment than saying it takes 2 years to speak Japanese. The more hours you put into practicing Japanese in a day or stay consistent throughout the week, the faster you’ll learn.

Ultimately, achieving a high level in Japanese takes time, as with other languages. A lot of people who live in Japan and studied the language for years might still say they have a long way to go, so you can’t expect instant results in a matter of weeks.

As a reference, we’ve broken down how long it takes to learn Japanese based on what you’re using the language for. Depending on your goal, you might want to focus on one language aspect (like speaking) more than the other.

GoalHow you’ll use JapaneseStudy Hours

How many hours a day should I study Japanese to become fluent?

The number of hours a day you need to study Japanese to become fluent depends on your personal goals, your current level of proficiency, and your preferred learning style. Can I become fluent in Japanese in six months?


While it’s possible to make significant progress in six months of intensive study, becoming fully fluent in Japanese within such a short period is unlikely. Achieving fluency in Japanese requires a deep understanding of the language, which takes time to develop. You can achieve conversational fluency in six months.

Working with a tutor or language exchange partner can help you learn Japanese faster and more effectively. A tutor can provide personalized instruction and feedback, while a language exchange partner can offer opportunities to practice speaking and listening skills with a native speaker.

How long does it take to learn Japanese kanji?

FSI considered Japanese a “super-hard language”, categorizing it in the same group as Arabic, Korean, Mandarin, and Cantonese.

Be warned: you are about to read the most groan-worthy Japanese dad jokes ever! 親父ギャグ (Oyaji gyagu), literally meaning “old man gags,” is the Japanese equivalent of “dad jokes.” They are characterized by cheesy puns, or ダジャレ in Japanese. Similar to English, Japanese puns are built on homophones, or words that sound the same but have different meanings.

Dad jokes are just as cheesy in Japanese as they are in any language, but they are a great way to learn about Japanese culture and humor while practicing informal sentence structures. Japanese dad jokes can help with picking up natural language through their use of non-literal, figurative language.

What Are Japanese Dad Jokes or 親父ギャグ (Oyaji Gagu)?

Most Japanese dad jokes use homophones, a fancy grammatical term for when two different words, with different meanings, sound very similar. Since the Japanese language only has a limited number of unique syllables to build words from, homophones end up being very common, and it’s quite easy to make corny jokes out of them. This is the basis of many dad jokes and ダジャレ in general.

Onomatopoeia, or the written form of action sounds, are abundant in the Japanese language, so they are another common component of dad jokes.

1. このステーキはすてき！(kono suteeki wa suteki!)

Romaji: Kono suteeki wa suteki!
Meaning: The steak is wonderful!
Joke Explanation:
Steak → ステーキ (suteeki)
Wonderful → ステキ (suteki)

A classic, simple homophone that relies on nearly identical sounds, and the best part is that it only requires JLPT N5 knowledge to understand! ステーキ, meaning beef steak, a dad’s favorite food, is said quickly in a shortened form to sound just like ステキ, which means lovely or wonderful.

ステキな isn’t a very natural way to describe delicious food, so the intentional word choice elicits the inevitable groan. For natural, casual ways to describe food, you can combine the prefixes めちゃ or マジで, meaning very, with おいしい or うまい, meaning tasty.

2. 美味すぎて、馬になった。(umasugite, uma ni natta.)

Romaji: umasugite, uma ni natta
Meaning: It was so delicious I turned into a horse.
Joke Explanation:
Delicious → 美味い (umai)
Horse → 馬 (uma)

The pun comes from the similar sounds of 馬 (uma), meaning horse, and 美味い (umai), meaning “delicious.” The joke also incorporates a bit of N4 grammar: the suffix すぎる (sugiru), which means “too much.”

For example, if you want to emphasize how cold it is outside on the first day of winter, you may say さむすぎる instead of just さむい. The て form lets you connect clauses fluidly, showing cause and relation or the order of events. 馬 is the corresponding second homophone, followed by なった, the past tense form of なる, meaning to become.

3. 土管の中でドッカーン (Dokan no naka de dokkaan.)

Romaji: Dokan no naka de dokkaan.
Meaning: Kaboom inside the clay pipe.
Joke Explanation:
Clay Pipe → 土管 (dokan)
Kaboom →ドッカーン

This one is a combination effect of onomatopoeia with homophones. This joke that relies on more advanced kanji & vocabulary (around N1 level), using the very particular word for clay / earthen pipe土管 to sound like the onomatopoeia ドッカーン. A very simple N5 grammatical structure using の中で as a prepositional phrase, denoting where the kaboom took place. What makes this joke a bit more difficult is the advanced-level vocab 土管, which you will probably never encounter unless you read construction signs.

4. 餃子を食べて、仰天！(gyoza o tabete, gyoten!)

Romaji: gyoza o tabete, gyoten!
Meaning: I ate the gyoza and was amazed!
Joke Explanation:
Gyoza → 餃子
Amazed → 仰天 (gyoten)

This dad joke is a simple homophone that rhymes the popular Japanese dumplings, gyoza, with the expression of amazement, gyoten. Once again, we see the て- form grammar connecting the two clauses.

To read, this joke relies on more niche N3-level kanji knowledge. While 餃子 may be easier for foodies to recognize, 仰天 is quite advanced for learners. Still, this dad joke is easy to remember for your next visit to a Chinese restaurant!

5. チーターが池におっこちーたー. (Chiitaa ga ike ni okkochiitaa.)

Romaji: Chiitaa ga ike ni okkochiitaa.
Meaning: The cheetah fell into the pond.
Joke Explanation:
Cheetah → チーター
Fall down → 落っこちる (okkochiru)

This is more of an N2-level joke because the dramatized, colloquial form of 落ちる used in this joke isn’t commonly learned or taught early on. The rest of the rhyme uses easier vocabulary and grammar. We see が used once again as a subject particle, describing what the cheetah is doing. Combining this with the kanji for pond, 池, and using に as a preposition for the direction of the cheetah sets us up for the punchline.

The informal past tense of “to fall down” sounds just like the katakana word for cheetah, if dragged out, completing our homophonic dad joke. Once again, 落っこちる is more of a spoken, dramatized version of 落ちる

6. イルカはいるか？(iruka wa iruka?)

Romaji: Iruka wa iruka
Meaning: Are there any dolphins?
Joke Explanation:
Dolphin → イルカ
there is (living subject) → いる

This joke is as easy and cheesy as it gets. イルカ is written in katakana mainly because the kanji is hard to read, so it’s more convenient and accessible. は is used as our subject particle, as the dolphins are the subject of our silly question. いる, the word for “there is” when referring to animate subjects, is given the informal suffix か to turn it into a question. Maybe use this dad joke when you visit the Sumida Aquarium near Tokyo Skytree to test some reactions.

7. 車で、来るまで待つ。(kuruma de, kuru made matsu.)

Romaji: kuruma de kuru made matsu
Meaning: I will wait until they come by car.
Joke Explanation:
Car → 車 (kuruma)
Come → 来る (kuru)
Until → まで

Great for beginners to stretch their minds, this one uses a somewhat clever homophone, relying on the connection between 来る and まで to form the punchline. A phonetic mirror, if executed perfectly, 来るまで should sound just like 車 being enunciated poorly. 待つ is an N5-level vocabulary word meaning to wait. まで has several grammatical uses, but here it signifies waiting for the preceding action to occur.

8. 歯科医師が司会した。(shikaishi ga shikaishita)

Romaji: shikaishi ga shikaishita
Meaning: The dentist moderated the meeting
Joke Explanation:
Dentist → 歯科医師 (shikaishi)
Moderated → 司会する (shikai suru)

Because of the vocabulary it uses, this joke might be around N2 level. It’s structurally similar to the homophone examples we explained earlier, but it requires advanced kanji & vocab knowledge. This joke rests on the past tense of 司会する (shikaisuru), which is 司会した (shikaishita), meaning “led” or “moderated”.

To pull this dad joke off, you must pronounce 司会した (shikaishita) to sound exactly like 歯科医師 (shikaishita), which takes some over-enunciation of the し in した.

9. 電話に出んわ (Denwa ni denwa)

Romaji: denwa ni denwa
Meaning: I won’t answer the phone.
Explanation:
Phone → 電話 (denwa)
Answer → 出る (deru)

While the grammar and vocabulary are quite simple, the use of a different Japanese dialect could confuse beginners. This dad joke uses the Kansai dialect, which you may hear in Osaka or around Kyoto. The punchline of the joke takes the standard phrase 電話に出ない, dropping ない (nai) and adding ん (n), a shortened negative form, and the Kansai suffix わ, used to express emphasis. Now, 出ない sounds like denwa, similar to the word for “phone” or “call.”

In English, depending on where you learned to speak, we all say things a bit differently. The same applies to Japan, where different regions have their own way of saying things. One of the main alternatives to standard Japanese is the rough-sounding Kansai dialect.

10. 私はニューヨークで入浴した。(watashi wa nyuu yooku de nyuuyokushita.)

Romaji: Watashi wa nyuu yooku de nyuyokushita
Meaning: I took a bath in New York.
Explanation:
Bathing (formal) → 入浴 (nyuuyoku)
New York → ニューヨーク

Although this joke is grammatically simple, the term 入浴 (nyuuyoku) is very formal and uses old kanji that you will likely only see at an onsen. If you stretch out 入浴 (nyuuyoku), it sounds like how you would pronounce New York in katakana: ニューヨーク (nyuuyooku).

Combining these two homophones with the particle で, which denotes the location of the action, means the bath was taken in New York. Onsen are where you might see this kanji used seriously, for example: 入浴時間 (nyuuyoku jikan), meaning bathing hours.

How to Make Your Own Japanese Dad Jokes

Since these jokes are great practice for your Japanese skills no matter your level, consider playing around and writing your own. Here are a few easy steps to get you started.


Pay attention to homophones. Japanese’s limited number of unique syllables naturally creates many homophones.

Use simple grammar structures. These jokes don’t require difficult grammar, so don’t be afraid to form sentences informally.

Use what you know. This is the best way to master a language; using what you have learned in your own way will lead to a strong acquisition of Japanese.


Conclusion: Dad Jokes are Great for Practicing Japanese!

Once you get the hang of these puns, it is fun to use the vocab and grammar that you are familiar with to construct your own. This is a very basic one:

Salmon roe → いくら
How much? → いくら
いくらはいくら？
How much is the salmon roe?

Expressing your sense of humor is a huge part of language learning and speaking Japanese more naturally! Jokes aren’t only fun; they can help you remember more words and express yourself more freely without sticking to rigid, literal definitions!

Sharing a laugh may be one of the best ways to practice Japanese!

The year might be drawing to a close, but it's a perfect time to do something new with your Japanese study! Take a look below at the latest list of Japanese learning resources, lovingly selected by our team, to help supercharge your Japanese study.

Activate Your Japanese!

Activate Your Japanese! is a 24-episode drama about a Vietnamese girl named Xuan who came to Japan to work in a hotel. It comes from Japan's national broadcasting network, known as NHK, which is known for producing quality video content about all sorts of topics. You can think of them as the BBC or CNN of Japan. In the drama, she encounters a sentient keychain, new friends, and lots of new Japanese. And as with any drama, there are elements of humor and romance that really make it entertaining.

Each video is divided into parts: The main skit, Today's Strategy, Onomatopoeia, and Welcome to My Japan. The main skit follows Xuan and her time adjusting to Japanese life, all while providing useful communication strategies. Next, the Today's Strategy section focuses on a useful communication strategy or phrase that Xuan utilized in the main skit. Plenty of examples are provided, making this part of each video particularly useful for learners. Then comes the Onomatopoeia bit, which introduces a common Japanese onomatopoeia. Again, several examples are provided to help reinforce how the word is used in real life. And finally, the Welcome to My Japan bit finishes off each video with a presentation of someone's life after coming to Japan. Many of these individuals immigrated to Japan for work and have lived in the country for several years. Their work, interests, and hobbies are highlighted in this section.

Every video in this series comes with translated captions and even a transcript, making it ideal for learners at level who want to practice reading or listening skills. But even if learning Japanese is not your main goal, the series can still be enjoyed purely as a drama for one's own entertainment. According to the site, this series will be available until 2027, so there's plenty of time to go through each of the 15-minute episodes.

Beyond Activate Your Japanese!, the NHK has a number of other resources for Japanese learners, like the Essential Japanese section, which provides survival phrases, and Easy Japanese: Conversation Lessons, which contains lots of learning content related to conversation practice. There's something for everyone, so check it out!
